question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align} \int_6^\infty \dfrac { 12}{x^2}\,\textrm{d}x &= \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_6^a \dfrac { 12}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = 12 \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_6^a x^{-2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = 12 \lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ \left( -x^{-1} \right) \right ]_6^a \\[5pt] & = -12 \cdot \lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ \dfrac{1}{x} \right ]_6^a \\[5pt] &= -12 \cdot \lim_{a \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac {1}{6}\right) \\[5pt] &= -12 \left(0 - \dfrac{1}{6}\right) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{ 2 }. \end{align}

question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align} \int_1^\infty \dfrac {2}{\sqrt{x^9}} \,\textrm{d}x &= \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_1^a \dfrac {2}{\sqrt{x^9}} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = 2 \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_1^a x^{-9/2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = 2\lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ -\dfrac{2}{7}x^{-7/2} \right ]_1^a \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{4}{7} \cdot \lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^7}} \right ]_1^a \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{4}{7} \cdot \lim_{a \to \infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a^7}} - \dfrac {1}{\sqrt{1^7}}\right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{4}{7} \left (0 - 1\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {4}{7}. \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=4t+3.$ Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}t} = 4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =4\textrm{d}t. \]

Since $u \to \infty$ when $t \to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=4t+3$ is as follows:

$t$ $0$ $\infty$
$u$ $3$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\[ \int_0^\infty \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{(4t+3)^3}} \,\textrm{d}t = \int_3^\infty \dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{u^3}} \,\textrm{d}u \]

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{(4t+3)^3}} \,\textrm{d}t &=\int_3^{\infty} \dfrac{3}{2\sqrt{u^3}} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\int_3^{\infty} \dfrac{3}{2}u^{-3/2} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_3^a \dfrac{3}{2}u^{-3/2} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[-3 u^{-1/2}\right]_3^a \\[5pt] &=-3 \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[u^{-1/2}\right]_3^a \\[5pt] &=-3\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right]\\[5pt] &=-3\cdot\left(0-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\sqrt{3}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=x^2+3.$ Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =2x\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $u \to \infty$ when $x \to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^2+3$ is as follows:

$x$ $0$ $\infty$
$u$ $3$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\[ \int_0^\infty \dfrac{54x}{(x^2+3)^{4}} \,\textrm{d}x = \int_3^\infty \dfrac{27}{u^{4}} \,\textrm{d}u \]

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{54x}{(x^2+3)^{4}} \,\textrm{d}x &=\int_3^{\infty} \dfrac{27}{u^{4}} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\int_3^{\infty} 27u^{-4} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_3^a 27u^{-4} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[-9 u^{-3}\right]_3^a \\[5pt] &=-9 \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[u^{-3}\right]_3^a \\[5pt] &=-9\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[\dfrac{1}{a^{3}} -\dfrac{1}{3^{3}} \right]\\[5pt] &=-9\cdot\left(0-\dfrac{1}{27}\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{3}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=2x+1.$ Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =2\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $u \to \infty$ when $x \to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2x+1$ is as follows:

$x$ $0$ $\infty$
$u$ $1$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\[ \int_0^\infty \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{(2x+1)^5}} \,\textrm{d}x = \int_1^\infty \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{u^5}} \,\textrm{d}u \]

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{(2x+1)^5}} \,\textrm{d}x &=\int_1^{\infty} \dfrac{3}{{u^{5/2}}} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\int_1^{\infty} 3u^{-5/2} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_1^a 3u^{-5/2} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[-2 u^{-3/2}\right]_1^a \\[5pt] &=-2 \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[u^{-3/2}\right]_1^a \\[5pt] &=-2\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[\dfrac{1}{a^{3/2}} -\dfrac{1}{1^{3/2}} \right]\\[5pt] &=-2\cdot\left(0-1\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution

question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=x^2+1.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u =x\,\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $ u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^2+1$ is as follows:

$x$ $0$ $\infty$
$u$ $1$ $\infty$
So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is \begin{align} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{(x^2+1)^3}} \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^3}} \,\textrm{d}u. \end{align}

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u^3}} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_1^a {u^{-3/2}} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ -2u^{-1/2} \right]_1^a\\[5pt] &= - \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u}} \right]_1^a\\[5pt] &=-\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}} - 1 \right)\\[5pt] &= - \left(0 - 1\right)\\[5pt] &=1. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution

question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=y^3-2.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}y}= 3y^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{3}\textrm{d}u =y^2\,\textrm{d}y. \]

Since $ u\to \infty $ when $y\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=y^3-2$ is as follows:

$y$ $3$ $\infty$
$u$ $25$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\begin{align} \displaystyle \int_3^\infty \dfrac{5y^2}{\left(y^3-2\right)^2} \,\textrm{d}y &=\int_{25}^\infty \dfrac{5}{u^2} \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\,\textrm{d}u\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{3}\int_{25}^\infty \dfrac{1}{u^2} \,\textrm{d}u. \end{align}

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_3^\infty \dfrac{5y^2}{\left(y^3-2\right)^2} \,\textrm{d}y &=\dfrac{5}{3}\int_{25}^\infty \dfrac{1}{u^2} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{3}\int_{25}^\infty u^{-2} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_{25}^a u^{-2} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \big[ -u^{-1} \big]_{25}^a\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{5}{3} \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{u}\right]_{25}^a\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{5}{3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{25} \right)\\[5pt] &= - \dfrac{5}{3}\left(0 - \dfrac{1}{25}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{15}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=4t+3.$ Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}t} = 4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =4\textrm{d}t. \]

Since $u \to -\infty$ when $t \to -\infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=4t+3$ is as follows:

$t$ $-\infty$ $-1$
$u$ $-\infty$ $-1$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\[ \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{10}{(4t+3)^4} \,\textrm{d}t = \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{5}{2u^4} \,\textrm{d}u \]

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{5}{2u^4} \,\textrm{d}u & =\dfrac{5}{2}\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^{-1} u^{-4} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{5}{2}\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{3}u^{-3} \right]_a^{-1}\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{5}{6}\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{u^3} \right]_a^{-1}\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{5}{6}\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{(-1)^3}- \dfrac{1}{a^3} \right]\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{5}{6}\cdot\left(-1-0\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{5}{6}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit

question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{-\infty}^{-2} \dfrac { 5}{x^5} \,\textrm{d}x & = 5\lim_{a \to -\infty}\int_{a}^{-2} \dfrac { 1}{x^5} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = 5\lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[-\dfrac {1}{4x^4} \right]_a^{-2} \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{5}{4}\lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[\dfrac {1}{x^4} \right]_a^{-2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{5}{4}\lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[\dfrac {1}{(-2)^4} -\dfrac {1}{a^4} \right] \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{5}{4}\lim_{a \to -\infty} \left(\dfrac {1}{16} - \dfrac {1}{a^4} \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{5}{4}\left(\dfrac {1}{16} - 0 \right) \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac {5}{64}. } \]

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit

question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=7x+3.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 7 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 7\,\textrm{d}u =\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $ u\to -\infty $ when $x\to -\infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=7x+3$ is as follows:

$x$ $-1$ $-\infty$
$u$ $-4$ $-\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\[ \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{(7x+3)^3} \,\textrm{d}x =\int_{-\infty}^{-4} \dfrac{1}{7u^3} \,\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{(7x+3)^3} \,\textrm{d}x &= \int_{-\infty}^{-4} \dfrac{1}{7u^3} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{7} \int_{-\infty}^{-4} u^{-3} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{7}\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_{a}^{-4} u^{-3} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{7}\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ - \dfrac {1}{2}u^{-2} \right]_{a}^{-4} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{ 14}\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac {1}{ u^2} \right]_{a}^{-4} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{ 14}\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac {1}{ (-4)^2}-\dfrac {1}{ a^2} \right]\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{ 14}\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left( \dfrac {1}{ 16}-\dfrac {1}{ a^2} \right)\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{ 14}\cdot\left( \dfrac {1}{ 16}-0 \right)\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{ 224}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=x^3-4.$ Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =3x^2\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $u \to -\infty$ when $x \to -\infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^3-4$ is as follows:

$x$ $-\infty$ $-2$
$u$ $-\infty$ $-12$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\[ \int_{-\infty}^{-2} \dfrac{9x^2}{(x^3-4)^2} \,\textrm{d}x = \int_{-\infty}^{-12} \dfrac{3}{u^2} \,\textrm{d}u \]

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{-12} \dfrac{3}{u^2} \,\textrm{d}u & =3\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^{-12} u^{-2} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=3\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ -u^{-1} \right]_a^{-12}\\[5pt] &=-3\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{u} \right]_a^{-12}\\[5pt] &=-3\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{(-12)}- \dfrac{1}{a} \right]\\[5pt] &=-3\cdot\left(-\dfrac{1}{12}-0\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{4}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit

question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{x^3} \,\textrm{d}x & =\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^{-1} x^{-3} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{2}x^{-2} \right]_a^{-1}\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{x^2} \right]_a^{-1}\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac{1}{(-1)^2}- \dfrac{1}{a^2} \right]\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 1\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit

question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\[ \eqalign{ \int_1^\infty -\dfrac {6}{\sqrt[5]x} \,\textrm{d}x & = -6\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty} \int_1^a\dfrac {1}{\sqrt[5]x} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = -6\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty}\left[\dfrac { 5}{4} x^{4/ 5} \right]_1^a \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{15}{2}\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty}\left[ x^{4/ 5} \right]_1^a \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac { 15}{2}\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty} \left( a^{4/ 5} -1\right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac { 15}{2}\cdot\infty\\[5pt] &=-\infty. } \] Therefore, the integral is divergent.

example.title: Identifying Divergent Improper Integrals

question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{6}^\infty \dfrac {\textrm{d}z}{z} & = \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{6}^a \dfrac {\textrm{d}z}{z}\\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to \infty} \left[\ln z \right]_{6}^a \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a \to \infty} \left(\ln a - \ln 6 \right) \\[5pt] &=\infty - \ln 6\\[5pt] &= \infty. } \]

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

example.title: Identifying Divergent Improper Integrals

question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=8-x^3.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= -3x^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac1 3 \,\textrm{d}u =x^2\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $ u\to \infty $ when $x\to -\infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=8-x^3$ is as follows: \[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline x& -1& -\infty\\ \hline u& 9& \infty\\ \hline \end{array} \] So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is \[ \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{8-x^3}} \,\textrm{d}x =\int_{\infty}^{9}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{u}} \right)\,\textrm{d}u=\dfrac{1}{3}\int_9^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u}} \,\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty.$ \begin{align} \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{8-x^3}} \,\textrm{d}x& = \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty} \int_9^{a}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{u}} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty} \left[2\sqrt{u}\right]_9^{a}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\lim_{a \to \infty} \left[\sqrt{a}-\sqrt 9\right]\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\infty\\[5pt] &=\infty. \end{align}

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

example.title: Identifying Divergent Improper Integrals

question.text:
Which of the following improper integrals are divergent?

  1. $\displaystyle \int_{10}^\infty \dfrac {1}{\sqrt{x-1}} \,\textrm{d}x$
  2. $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{x} \,\textrm{d}x$
  3. $\displaystyle \int_{1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x$
question.explanation:
Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have \begin{align} \int_{10}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x - 1}} \,\textrm{d}x & = \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{10}^{a} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x - 1}} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to \infty} \left[2\sqrt {x-1} \right]_{10}^a \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a \to \infty} \left(2\sqrt{a-1} - 2\sqrt{10-1} \right) \\[5pt] &=\lim_{a \to \infty} \left(2\sqrt{a-1} - 6 \right) \\[5pt] &= \infty, \end{align} so the integral diverges.

For the second integral, we have \begin{align} \displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{x} \,\textrm{d}x & = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \int_{a}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{x} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[ \ln|x| \right]_{a}^{-1} \\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to -\infty} (\ln|-1| - \ln|a|)\\[5pt] & = -\infty, \end{align} so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have \begin{align} \int_{1}^{\infty} \dfrac{1}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x & = \lim_{a \to \infty} \int_{1}^{a} \dfrac{1}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to \infty} \left[-\dfrac{1}{x}\right]_{1}^{a} \\[5pt] & = \lim_{a \to \infty} \left(-\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{1} \right)\\[5pt] & = 1, \end{align} so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integrals I and II are divergent.

example.title: Identifying Divergent Improper Integrals

question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{1}{3x+1} \,\textrm{d}x &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_0^a \dfrac{1}{3x+1} \,\textrm{d}x\\ &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ \dfrac13 \cdot \ln|3x+1| \right]_0^a\\[5pt] &= \dfrac13 \cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ \ln|3x+1| \right]_0^a\\[5pt] &=\dfrac13 \cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left(\ln|3a+1|-\ln(1)\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac13 \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left( \ln|3a+1| \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac13 \cdot \left( \infty \right)\\[5pt] &=\infty. \end{align*} Therefore, the integral is divergent.
